# 🛰️ First Satellite vs. Latest Satellite

## 🌍 SPUTNIK 1 — The World's First Satellite (1957)

Sputnik 1 was the first artificial Earth satellite, launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.

### Size & Weight
It was only about the size of a beach ball — 22.8 inches (58 cm) in diameter — and weighed just 183.9 pounds (83.6 kg), orbiting the Earth in around 98 minutes.

### Technology & Payload
It was an extremely simple satellite — a metal sphere with four long antennas protruding from it, containing a thermometer, a fan, a radio transmitter, batteries, and little else.

### Mission
The only cargo onboard Sputnik was a low-power radio transmitter, which broadcast a beeping noise at regular intervals — a signal that could be heard by radio listeners around the world.

### Lifespan
The satellite transmitters operated for three weeks, until the on-board chemical batteries failed. The orbit of the then inactive satellite decayed 92 days after launch (January 4, 1958) after having completed about 1,400 orbits of the Earth.

### Orbit
Sputnik 1's orbit was elliptical — approximately 230 km from Earth at its closest point (perigee) and 940 km away at its furthest point (apogee).

### Launch Vehicle
It was launched on a **Modified SS-6 (Sapwood)** rocket from Tyuratam (Baikonur Cosmodrome), USSR.

### Historical Impact
The satellite's success was unanticipated by the United States, which precipitated the American Sputnik crisis and triggered the start of the **Space Race**.

---

## 🚀 VIASAT-3 F3 — One of the Latest Major Satellites (2026)

ViaSat-3 Flight 3 (VS-3 F3) successfully launched from **Kennedy Space Center** in Florida aboard a **SpaceX Falcon Heavy** rocket on **April 29, 2026**.

### Size & Weight
It is built on Boeing's high-power **702MP+ platform**, which supports power-intensive payloads and features an all-electric propulsion system — allowing for more precise orbital positioning and a lighter overall weight. For comparison, modern-day geostationary communications satellites can weigh as much as **7,000 kg** — over eighty times as much as Sputnik 1.

### Technology & Payload
The ViaSat-3 class of Ka-band satellites is expected to provide unprecedented capabilities in terms of service speed and flexibility for a satellite platform. Boeing scaled the platform to accommodate massive solar arrays and advanced electronics capable of delivering over **1 terabit per second** of network capacity.

### Mission & Coverage
The ViaSat-3 constellation consists of three separate satellites, each designed to provide coverage to a region: ViaSat-3 F1 covers the Americas; ViaSat-3 F2 covers Europe, the Middle East and Africa; and ViaSat-3 F3 covers the **Asia-Pacific** region.

The satellites are intended to provide broadband connectivity with speeds of 100-plus megabits per second to homes, businesses, commercial aircraft, government and defense markets, and maritime enterprises.

### Orbit
The Falcon Heavy rocket reduces time to orbit by delivering the satellite to a more favorable transfer orbit, where the satellite's **electric propulsion** takes over to place ViaSat-3 F3 in **geostationary orbit**.

### Lifespan & Service
Once operational, it will allow Viasat to dynamically shift capacity to where it is needed most — whether for a commercial airliner over the Pacific or a naval vessel in a remote corridor — ensuring bandwidth is never wasted and performance remains consistent even during peak usage.

---

| **Launch Date** | October 4, 1957 | April 29, 2026 |

| **Launch Vehicle** | Modified SS-6 Rocket | SpaceX Falcon Heavy |
| **Weight** | ~83.6 kg | ~6,000–7,000 kg class |
| **Shape/Form** | 58 cm metal sphere | Large geostationary spacecraft with massive solar arrays |

| **Payload** | Radio transmitter & thermometer | Ka-band broadband internet (>1 Tbps capacity) |

| **Lifespan** | ~3 weeks (transmitting), ~92 days in orbit | Designed for ~15+ years |
| **Data Transmitted** | Simple radio beep | Over **1 Terabit per second** |
| **Coverage** | Covered most of Earth's surface by orbit path | Asia-Pacific region (geostationary) |

---

## 🔑 Key Takeaway
The leap from Sputnik 1 to ViaSat-3 F3 represents nearly **70 years of extraordinary innovation**. Sputnik was a simple metal ball that beeped — proof that humanity could reach orbit. ViaSat-3 F3 is a multi-ton engineering marvel delivering terabits of internet capacity across an entire continent, with advanced electric propulsion and decades of planned service life.
